newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin orders cabinet reshuffle to boost reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin orders cabinet reshuffle to boost reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, stamping his authority on Russia after months of illness, ordered a far-reaching cabinet reshuffle on Tuesday which opened the way for a new burst of radical economic reform.

Flying in the face of the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament and many of the voters who re-elected him president last July, Yeltsin gave loyal reformist aide Anatoly Chubais a chance to shape policy in a new-look government.

A presidential decree published by Yeltsin's press service ordered Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to come up with cabinet proposals within a week. Itar-Tass news agency said Yeltsin may announce the changes by the end of this week.
But analysts said that Chernomyrdin's new first deputy Chubais would be the driving force behind the changes.
In another step clearly aimed to free the hands of the reinforced cabinet, Yeltsin appointed his ghost-writer Valentin Yumashev, 39, to replace Chubais as his chief of staff.

Yumashev, a former journalist with no bureaucratic background, looks likely to run the Kremlin administration as Yeltsin's personal chancellery rather than as a "parallel government" as it was considered by opponents under Chubais.

Chubais, who spearheaded privatisation from 1991, was dropped from the government at the start of 1996 because of intense public hatred of his policies -- a liability for Yeltsin who faced a strong communist electoral challenge.

Yeltsin brought him back into the government on Friday, winning approval from foreign investors but raising protests from opposition politicians and some commentators, who said the 41-year-old privatisation guru had let a minority rob Russia.

The president, accused by critics of letting policy drift while he recovered from heart problems for six months, last week blamed Chernomyrdin's government for the country's ills, which include huge backlogs in tax payments, wages and pensions.

Pledging to restore order, fight corruption and revive the devastated economy, Yeltsin said in a state-of-the-nation speech designed to mark his return to the helm that he would reorganise the cabinet and bring in new "competent and energetic" people.
Tuesday's decree involves a radical reorganisation of the government, which has more than 30 ministers and many agencies and departments in a hangover from the bureaucratic Soviet era.
It does not mean the formal resignation of the cabinet but makes clear that all jobs apart from Chernomyrdin's and, by implication, Chubais' are potentially up for grabs.
Kremlin sources said that the reshuffle would be "serious" and was taking so long because many people would have to be axed, moved, or otherwise accommodated.

Yeltsin's decision to give Chernomyrdin a free hand in picking ministers -- old or new -- for his cabinet won some praise from his old-time liberal ally, Yegor Gaidar, who oversaw the initial phase of Russia's economic reform.
"It is a technically correct and sensible step which will allow to carry out the structural changes in the government promptly," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

But another prominent liberal leader, Grigory Yavlinsky, said it was too early to draw conclusions. "It is not clear who will join the government other than the promises that they will be 'young and energetic'," he told Interfax news agency.

The main opposition Communist Party reacted cautiously. Gennady Seleznyov, speaker of the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament, said it was designed to pre-empt a demand from the chamber for the government's dismissal and that parliament should be consulted over the new positions.
Yeltsin's decree said the government would have one first deputy prime minister instead of four and the number of deputy prime ministers would be cut from the current nine.
The number of ministries -- and of ministers -- would also be cut and some of the ministries reorganised.
